relationship: contrasting denials of prophetic status with an agricultural occupation
rationale: Zechariah's speaker denies being a prophet and identifies himself as a worker of the earth amid the exposure of lying prophets. Amos likewise says he was no prophet or prophet's son but a herder and fig worker, then recounts the Lord's call. The denial-and-occupation pattern is shared, while its contexts and force differ.
source_text: He will say, ‘I am no prophet; I am a man who works the earth, because a man begot me from my youth.’

target_units.text: Amos answered Amaziah, “I was no prophet or prophet’s son, but a goat herder and one who scratches sycamore figs,
and the Lord took me from the sheep, and the Lord said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’

relationship: later Scripture quotation about striking the shepherd and dispersing sheep
rationale: Zechariah commands a sword against shepherds and the striking of shepherds with sheep torn away. Jesus in Matthew introduces a written saying that the shepherd will be struck and the flock scattered, applying it to His disciples' coming failure. The shared action and flock consequence connect the texts while plural shepherds and singular shepherd remain distinct.
source_text: Sword, awake against My shepherds, against the man who is My fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty! Strike the shepherds and tear away the sheep; I will bring My hand against the shepherds.

target_units.text: Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will stumble because of Me this night, for it is written: ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’
But after I am raised, I will go ahead of you to Galilee.”

relationship: later written saying about the struck shepherd and scattered sheep
rationale: Mark introduces Jesus' warning with a written saying about striking the shepherd and scattering the sheep. Zechariah likewise joins struck shepherds with sheep torn away. The correspondence is explicit in the actions, while Mark's singular shepherd and subsequent resurrection promise retain their own wording.
source_text: Sword, awake against My shepherds, against the man who is My fellow citizen, says the Lord Almighty! Strike the shepherds and tear away the sheep; I will bring My hand against the shepherds.

target_units.text: Jesus said to them, “You will all stumble, because it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
But after I am raised, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.”

relationship: judgment represented through divided portions and a surviving remnant
rationale: Zechariah divides the land's people into two parts that fail and a third that remains. Ezekiel divides symbolic hairs into quarters for judgment and gathers a few into his cloak. Both use measured portions to depict destruction and survival, without equating Zechariah's thirds with Ezekiel's quarters.
source_text: Throughout the land, says the Lord, the two parts will be destroyed and fail, but the third will remain in it.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, take a sword sharper than a barber’s razor. Obtain it for yourself and pass it over your head and your beard. Take a balance with weights and divide the hairs;

burn a quarter with fire inside the city when the days of siege are complete. Take a quarter and burn it up in its midst; cut down a quarter with the sword around it, and scatter a quarter to the wind. I will draw a sword after them.
Take a few of them in number and gather them into your cloak.
Take some of these again, cast them into the fire, and burn them in the fire. From it fire will go out. And you will say to the entire house of Israel,

relationship: God's people tested by fire like silver
rationale: Zechariah promises leading the remaining third through fire and refining it as silver. The psalm likewise tells God that He tested His people by fire as silver is tested and brought them through affliction. The refining comparison is explicit in both.
source_text: I will lead the third through fire, refine them with fire as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested. He will call on My name, and I will listen to him and say, ‘This is My people,’ and he will say, ‘The Lord is my God.’”

target_units.text: For Thou didst test us, God; Thou didst try us by fire as silver is tried by fire.
Thou broughtest us into the trap; Thou didst place afflictions upon our back.
Thou madest human beings mount our heads; we passed through fire and water, and Thou broughtest us out to refreshment.

relationship: purification of people compared with refining gold and silver
rationale: Zechariah compares the surviving people's testing with the refining of silver and gold. Malachi likewise describes a smelting fire and purification of Levi's sons as gold and silver. Both apply metal refining to people, with distinct named groups.
source_text: I will lead the third through fire, refine them with fire as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested. He will call on My name, and I will listen to him and say, ‘This is My people,’ and he will say, ‘The Lord is my God.’”

target_units.text: And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearance? For he enters like a smelting fire and like launderers’ herb.

He will sit, smelting and purifying as with silver and gold. He will cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver, and they will be those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness.

relationship: reciprocal declaration that God and His people belong to one another
rationale: Zechariah ends the refining promise with God saying 'This is My people' and the people's response that the Lord is their God. Hosea likewise has God declare 'You are My people' and the answer 'Thou art the Lord my God.' The reciprocal formula directly corresponds.
source_text: I will lead the third through fire, refine them with fire as silver is refined and test them as gold is tested. He will call on My name, and I will listen to him and say, ‘This is My people,’ and he will say, ‘The Lord is my God.’”

target_units.text: I will sow her for Myself upon the land, show mercy to Not Shown Mercy and say to Not My People, ‘You are My people.’ He will say, ‘Thou art the Lord my God!’”

relationship: the Lord's approaching day in Jerusalem's judgment setting
rationale: Zechariah announces days of the Lord before describing war against Jerusalem. Joel likewise announces the near Lord's day amid judgment and the Lord's voice from Jerusalem. Both locate the approaching divine day within the city's wider judgment and deliverance setting, with spoils specified in Zechariah.
source_text: Look, days of the Lord are coming, and your spoils will be divided within you.

target_units.text: Sounds rang out in the Valley of Judgment, because the Lord’s day is near in the Valley of Judgment.
The sun and moon will grow dark, and the stars will sink their brightness.
The Lord will cry out from Zion and give His voice from Jerusalem; heaven and earth will shake. But the Lord will spare His people, and the Lord will strengthen the sons of Israel.

relationship: same-book gathering of all nations against Jerusalem
rationale: Chapter 14 announces the Lord gathering all nations against Jerusalem for war. Chapter 12 likewise describes all earth's nations gathering against her. The repeated gathering identifies a shared conflict setting without collapsing the different ensuing details.
source_text: I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for war. The city will be captured, the houses plundered and the women violated. Half the city will go into captivity, but the remnant of My people will certainly not be destroyed from the city.

target_units.text: On that day I will make Jerusalem a trampled stone for all the nations. Everyone trampling her will mock in mockery, and all the earth’s nations will gather against her.

relationship: survivors remain in Jerusalem through the crisis
rationale: Zechariah says that despite capture and captivity the remnant of God's people will not be destroyed from the city. Joel likewise promises one who escapes on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem amid the Lord's day. Both explicitly retain survival in that place.
source_text: I will gather all the nations against Jerusalem for war. The city will be captured, the houses plundered and the women violated. Half the city will go into captivity, but the remnant of My people will certainly not be destroyed from the city.

target_units.text: Everyone who calls upon the Lord’s name will be saved, for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be one who escapes, as the Lord said, and bearers of good news whom the Lord has called.”

relationship: the Lord intervenes as the decisive agent in battle
rationale: Zechariah announces the Lord going out and drawing up for battle among the nations. Exodus' song likewise names the Lord as shattering wars and praises His right hand for shattering enemies. Both portray divine action against opposing forces, with different battle scenes.
source_text: The Lord will go out and draw up for battle among those nations, as on the day of His battle formation on a day of war.

target_units.text: The Lord shatters wars; the Lord is His name.
Pharaoh’s chariots and his host He has cast into the sea; chosen riders, officers, He has drowned in the Red Sea.
With the sea He covered them; they sank into the deep as a stone.
Thy right hand, O Lord, has been glorified in strength; Thy right hand, O Lord, has shattered enemies.

relationship: the Mount of Olives in a scene connected with divine coming
rationale: Zechariah places the Lord's standing feet on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem. Acts locates Jesus' departure and the promise of His return at Olivet near Jerusalem. The named mountain and coming-related scene connect the passages; Acts does not narrate Zechariah's mountain splitting.
source_text: On that day His feet will stand on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem to the east. The Mount of Olives will split, half of it toward the east and half toward the sea—a very great chasm; half the mountain will incline north and half south.

target_units.text: After saying these things, He was lifted up as they watched, and a cloud took Him from their sight.
As they were gazing into heaven while He went, look—two men stood beside them in white garments.
They said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw Him go into heaven.”
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath’s journey away.

relationship: the Lord's coming accompanied by holy ones
rationale: Zechariah announces the coming of the Lord his God with all the holy ones. Paul likewise speaks of the coming of the Lord Jesus with all His saints. The stated accompaniment closely corresponds while each passage's designation of the Lord is preserved.
source_text: The ravine of My mountains will be blocked; the mountain ravine will be joined as far as Iasol and blocked as it was blocked in the days of the earthquake, in the days of Oziah king of Judah. The Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him.

target_units.text: so as to establish your hearts blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all His saints. Amen.

relationship: an earthquake remembered in the reign of Judah's king
rationale: Zechariah recalls the earthquake in the days of Oziah king of Judah. Amos dates his words two years before the earthquake in the days of Uzziah king of Judah. Both connect prophetic material with an earthquake and a named Judean reign; their name forms and relative dates are retained as supplied.
source_text: The ravine of My mountains will be blocked; the mountain ravine will be joined as far as Iasol and blocked as it was blocked in the days of the earthquake, in the days of Oziah king of Judah. The Lord my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him.

target_units.text: The words of Amos that came among nakkarim from Tekoa, which he saw concerning Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.

relationship: light extending beyond the ordinary day-and-night pattern
rationale: Zechariah describes a day known to the Lord, neither day nor night, with light toward evening. Isaiah likewise promises the Lord as everlasting light beyond ordinary sunlight and moonlight. Both describe exceptional illumination in restoration, without making Zechariah's one day an explicit statement of everlasting duration.
source_text: It will last one day, and that day is known to the Lord, neither day nor night; toward evening there will be light.

target_units.text: The sun will not be your light by day, nor will the rising moon light your night. Instead, the Lord will be your everlasting light and God your glory.
For your sun will not set, and your moon will not fail. The Lord will be your everlasting light, and your days of mourning will be fulfilled.

relationship: life-associated water flowing from the holy center toward the sea
rationale: Zechariah promises living water from Jerusalem toward two seas. Ezekiel describes water from the sacred house flowing toward the sea and bringing life wherever the river comes. Both connect outward-flowing water and life with the holy center, preserving their different routes.
source_text: On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, half into the first sea and half into the last sea; it will be so in summer and spring.

target_units.text: He brought me to the house’s vestibules, and look—water was flowing out beneath the open court toward the east, for the house’s front faced east. The water was descending from the right side, from the south toward the altar.
He brought me out by the north gate and led me around outside to the court’s gate facing east. Look—the water was flowing down from the right side.
As the man went out opposite, with a measure in his hand, he measured a thousand with the measure and went through the water—water of release.
He measured a thousand and went through water up to the thighs. He measured a thousand and went through water up to the waist.
He measured a thousand and could not go through, for the water surged violently like the rush of a torrent that they will not cross.
He said to me, “Have you seen, son of man?” Then he led me to the river’s edge.
As I returned, look—very many trees were on the river’s edge, on both sides.
He said to me, “This water flowing out into eastern Galilee was descending into Arabia and coming as far as the sea, to the water of the outlet; it will heal the waters.

Every life among the swarming living creatures will live wherever the river comes. There will be very many fish there, because this water has arrived there, and it will become healthy and live. Everything over which the river comes will live.
